Q: What is the difference between WS_POPUP and WS_OVERLAPPED without titlebar? A:

Are the actual frames different if I try to extend the frames using DwmExtendFrameIntoClientArea?

Yes. Microsoft explains:

Starting with Windows Vista, removing the standard frame by simply returning 0 when the wParam is TRUE does not affect frames that are extended into the client area using the DwmExtendFrameIntoClientArea function. Only the standard frame will be removed.

And when should I try to use each style?

Setting aside any issue with extended frames, the choice between removing the frame (via WM_NCCALCSIZE) or creating a window with a frame (with WS_POPUP) is largely about expressing the intent.

The window styles are a weird, non-orthogonal, and incomplete set, so it can be hard to express intent. As a first cut:

  • WS_OVERLAPPEDWINDOW for top-level windows without an owner other than the desktop.
  • WS_POPUP for temporary windows that are owned by another, like dialog boxes, tool tips, and tool palettes.
  • WS_CHILD for widgets that reside in the parent window's client area.

There have always been exceptions, like a dialog box that is the main top-level window of an application.

In your case, it seems like you want a top-level window without the standard frame.

  • An un-owned WS_POPUP window gives that directly, so that would be my choice.

  • It could be argued that it's clearer to create it with WS_OVERLAPPEDWINDOW, as that expresses the intent of having a top-level window. Unfortunately, that requires extra, non-obvious work to remove the frame with a WM_NCCALCSIZE handler.

(Unlike WS_OVERLAPPEDWINDOW, WS_OVERLAPPED doesn't include WS_CAPTION nor any type of a border, so you'd think you could choose that instead, but CreateWindowExW quietly adds WS_CAPTION and WS_EX_WINDOWEDGE if you specify just WS_OVERLAPPED, so you'd still have to remove the frame.)

Q: How can I debug a single thread in Visual Studio? A:

Here's what I did:

  1. Set a conditional breakpoint that I knew would only hit on the thread that I was looking for.

  2. Once the breakpoint hits and you are in the thread you want, in the Visual Studio Threads window (while debugging, Debug -> Windows -> Threads), Ctrl + A (to select all threads), and then Ctrl + click the thread you are currently on. You should have all threads except the one you want to debug selected.

  3. Right-click, and choose "Freeze".

Now, Visual Studio will only step through the thawed thread. It seems to be much slower when doing this, presumably because it has to loop through all of the frozen threads, but it brought some sanity to my multi-threaded debugging.

Q: How to unnest a list-column as new rows in pre-existing columns? A:

You can try

id <- 1:nrow(ex)
na.omit(do.call(rbind,c(split(ex[-3],id), setNames(ex[["z"]],id))[order(rep(id,2))]))

which gives

# A tibble: 7 × 2
  x           y
  <chr>   <dbl>
1 Q      0.633 
2 F      0.5   
3 E      0.404 
4 A     -0.106 
5 J      1.51  
6 A     -0.2   
7 D     -0.0947
